Leesburg is two wildlife towns wearing one name. Downtown, the colonial and early-republic core along King Street holds some of the oldest housing in Loudoun County — brick and log construction from the 1700s and 1800s, tall chimneys, and attics that have been bat habitat, on and off, for two hundred years. Tuscarora Creek cuts through the middle of it, and the raccoons treat the creek as a highway from the wooded bluffs at Ball's Bluff straight into those downtown roofs. Then there is the Leesburg of Exeter, Greenway Farms, Potomac Crossing, and the Lansdowne edge — newer suburbs where the calls are squirrels at the soffit line, raccoons in chimneys each spring, and moles working the irrigated lawns along the community trails.

Growth is the pressure underneath all of it. Every wooded lot cleared west and south of town pushes its resident wildlife into the standing neighbourhoods, and the green corridors that remain — the creek bottoms, the Ida Lee Park woods, the W&OD Trail's tree line — concentrate what is left right against people's back fences. Our Leesburg work tracks that map: historic-fabric sealing downtown, where the materials and methods have to respect a 250-year-old roofline, and fast, thorough exclusion in the suburbs, where the animals are simply following the tree canopy from yard to yard.
Leesburg.extendedBody:
Sealing a downtown Leesburg roof without scarring it

Leesburg's historic district homes were built before soffits were sealed systems — eaves were ventilated by design, mortar is soft lime, and most rooflines have been altered in stages since before the Civil War. Bats enter at ridge and chimney-shoulder gaps you can barely see from the ground; raccoons use the bigger failures where additions meet the original house. We survey the full junction map of a house like this, seal with materials matched to the fabric, and fit chimney caps that read as part of the house, not hardware bolted onto it. Bat work is exclusion only, and full exclusions are timed around the summer maternity season so flightless young are never sealed inside.

Suburban Leesburg: canopy streets and chimney dens

In Exeter, Greenway Farms, and Potomac Crossing, the pattern is newer but just as consistent: gray squirrels commuting along the street canopy and chewing in at soffit returns, raccoon mothers denning in uncapped chimneys every spring, skunks under the low decks, and moles tunnelling the watered lawns. Every job is handled by an operator holding a Commercial Nuisance Animal Permit (CNAP) issued by the Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources. Virginia treats raccoons and skunks as rabies-vector species, and our answer for them is the same downtown or out: exclusion, sealing, and cleanup — the den made unusable, not just emptied.

What a Leesburg inspection covers

Roofline and chimney first, then the foundation and crawlspace entries at grade, porch and deck voids, and the attic itself for droppings, staining, and nesting depth — which tells us how many seasons the problem has been running. Creek-side and trail-side homes get an extra pass along the lot line, because in Leesburg the habitat corridor behind the house is usually the reason the house has a problem.

Middleburg runs on horses, and horses shape its wildlife work. The hunt-country estates around the village carry miles of stone wall, bank barns, run-in sheds, and stable yards — groundhog burrows under every wall line and barn bank, raccoon dens in barn lofts and unused outbuildings, skunks under tack-room floors, and foxes denning along the Goose Creek headwater pastures, which is fine right up until the fox den is under the kennel fence. The village itself is small and old: stone and brick homes from the 1700s and 1800s whose attics hold bat colonies that predate everyone who has ever complained about them.

Our calls here are property calls more than house calls. An estate inspection walks the route an animal actually uses — woods to pasture to barn to house — because sealing the residence while the barn loft stays open accomplishes very little on fifty acres. In the village, the work is finer: sealing historic stone and brick against bats and squirrels without visible patching, capping tall chimneys, and clearing raccoons from the outbuildings and carriage houses that stand behind nearly every in-town property.
Middleburg.extendedBody:
Barns, stone walls, and the groundhog economy of hunt country

Groundhogs are the estate animal of Middleburg. They burrow under stone walls, barn banks, run-in sheds, and the edges of riding rings, and a working farm can host a dozen systems at once. Most are harmless tenants of the far fence lines, and we will tell you which ones to leave alone. The ones that matter are under structures — a burrow system beneath a barn bank or a stable slab undermines it season by season, and in horse country a collapsed run in a paddock is a veterinary bill, not a nuisance. Those get removed, the runs collapsed and backfilled, and the vulnerable edges screened so the system is not simply re-let.

Bats in the village, raccoons everywhere

Middleburg's stone and brick homes, and the big estate houses around it, hold some of the oldest bat colonies in the county — attics and unused chimneys that have hosted summer colonies for generations. Exclusion is the only answer, timed around the maternity season so the young are never sealed in, and on historic fabric it is done with matched materials and custom work at the chimney shoulders and eave junctions. Raccoons split the difference between the barns and the houses, denning in lofts all winter and in chimneys every spring. Our operators hold a Commercial Nuisance Animal Permit (CNAP) from the Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources, and Virginia's rabies-vector species — raccoons and skunks — are handled by exclusion and sealing, never by a relocation promise.

What an estate inspection looks like

We start at the house: roofline, chimneys, attic. Then the outbuildings in the order an animal would use them — barn loft, equipment sheds, run-ins, kennels — and the wall lines and banks where burrows undermine structures. You get a property map of what is active, what is structural risk, and what can be left exactly as it is. On a hunt-country property, that honesty about what to leave alone is worth as much as the trapping.
